title: Wall Street Week | India’s Growth Test, Bangalore’s Infrastructure Problem, Cricket Attracts Capital
title_cn: Wall Street Week | India’s Growth Test, Bangalore’s Infrastructure Problem, Cricket Attracts Capital
summary: This week, a special edition of Wall Street Week from the fastest growing large economy in the world: India. The country's technology sector has helped power its growth, but its success has led to uneven progress that could turn its strengths into weaknesses. Bangalore became India’s tech capital by attracting global investment and growing a deep talent pool, but infrastructure and policies to support the expansion have struggled to keep up. Plus, can Hyderabad overtake Bangalore as India’s leading tech city? Later, Blackstone’s investment in Royal Challengers Bengaluru reflects just how much potential India’s sports and entertainment economy has. This version corrects a map of India. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: How India Turned Cricket Into A Billion Dollar Business
title_cn: How India Turned Cricket Into A Billion Dollar Business
summary: India’s obsession with cricket has helped turn the Indian Premier League into one of the world’s most valuable sports leagues, attracting foreign investors like Blackstone. With only 10 teams serving a country of roughly 1.5 billion people, investors see scarcity, rising media consumption and India’s economic growth as powerful drivers of team valuations.  (Source: Bloomberg)

title: General Atlantic CEO Sees Long-Term AI Opportunity
title_cn: General Atlantic CEO Sees Long-Term AI Opportunity
summary:
General Atlantic CEO Bill Ford says accelerating innovation and entrepreneurship have created one of the strongest environments for growth investing in his three decades in the business, with opportunities spanning the US, Middle East, Asia and Latin America. Ford tells David Gura and Christina Ruffini on Bloomberg This Weekend that geopolitical risks are reshaping global supply chains but not reversing globalization, while AI should continue creating investment opportunities despite periods of overvaluation and concerns about safety.

At the 2026 Qatar Economic Forum, UNGA Special Edition; Powered by Bloomberg. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Why India’s Big Tech Companies Are Betting on Hyderabad
title_cn: Why India’s Big Tech Companies Are Betting on Hyderabad
summary: Hyderabad has spent decades building the talent, infrastructure and business climate to compete with Bangalore, attracting major tech firms while becoming a hub for life sciences. But AI now threatens some of the lower-cost IT work that helped fuel its rise. The test is whether Hyderabad can use its talent base to move from supporting global innovation to creating more of its own. This version corrects a map of India. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Qatar Says LNG Damage May Take Years to Repair
title_cn: Qatar Says LNG Damage May Take Years to Repair
summary:
Joining Bloomberg This Weekend, Qatar Central Bank Governor and Qatar Investment Authority Chairman Sheikh Bandar bin Mohammed bin Saoud Al-Thani says damage to the country’s LNG facilities could take two to three years to repair, with the conflict contributing to a 7% economic contraction even as the non-hydrocarbon economy grows. He says Qatar’s strong fiscal position has allowed QIA to continue investing globally, with technology and AI among its major areas of focus, while the central bank is deploying AI across its own operations.

At the 2026 Qatar Economic Forum, UNGA Special Edition; Powered by Bloomberg.
 (Source: Bloomberg)

title: State Street Sees Resilience Driving Portfolios
title_cn: State Street Sees Resilience Driving Portfolios
summary:
State Street Investment Management CEO Yie-Hsin Hung says investors have entered an era where resilient portfolios are increasingly important as higher capital costs, geopolitical tensions and technological change create a wider range of potential outcomes. Hung tells Bloomberg This Weekend hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini that institutional investors are adding liquidity and other portfolio buffers, while State Street is also expanding access to private markets and providing the default ETF for the US government's Trump Accounts program.

At the 2026 Qatar Economic Forum, UNGA Special Edition; Powered by Bloomberg.
 (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Rubio Takes on Expansive Foreign Policy Role
title_cn: Rubio Takes on Expansive Foreign Policy Role
summary:
Bloomberg News State Department reporter Eric Martin joins Bloomberg This Weekend and says Secretary of State Marco Rubio has embraced an unusually broad portfolio in the Trump administration, simultaneously serving as national security adviser while taking leading roles on Venezuela, Cuba and other foreign-policy priorities. Martin tells hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini that Rubio has largely worked behind the scenes on Iran while adapting his positions to his executive-branch role, a shift examined in Bloomberg Businessweek’s recent profile of the secretary.

At the 2026 Qatar Economic Forum, UNGA Special Edition; Powered by Bloomberg. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Can India Turn Its Promise Into Prosperity?
title_cn: Can India Turn Its Promise Into Prosperity?
summary: Blackstone COO Jon Gray says India’s young population, expanding middle class and improving infrastructure are drawing interest from global investors. But India’s demographic advantage also creates pressure: millions of young people graduate every year, while formal-sector job creation has not kept pace with their skills and expectations. At the same time, Indian states are competing aggressively for investment by cutting regulatory barriers, building industrial infrastructure and targeting sectors from electronics to semiconductors. The question is whether India can turn its scale, talent and investment momentum into enough productive jobs to sustain its growth. This version corrects a map of India. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: India’s Silicon Valley Is Straining Under Its Own Growth
title_cn: India’s Silicon Valley Is Straining Under Its Own Growth
summary: Bangalore helped turn India into a global hub for software services, tech talent and outsourcing, building an ecosystem that now supports multinational firms, domestic startups and capital. But the city’s success has also become one of its biggest weaknesses. India still lacks the depth of capital available in the US and China, while Bangalore’s physical infrastructure has struggled to keep pace with private-sector growth. At the same time, southern India’s rising economic power is colliding with demographic and political shifts that could threaten its representation in the country’s Central Government, which helps support the growth that cities like Bangalore have enjoyed. This version corrects a map of India. (Source: Bloomberg)
